title: Lena Maris (museum curator)
biography_text:
Lena Maris (born 12 March 1983) is a museum curator known for her work in regional history collections and community-focused exhibition design. She serves as the lead Museum Curator at the Harborview Museum of Local History, a mid-sized institution located in the fictional coastal city of Harborview. Her work focuses on organizing, preserving, and interpreting objects related to maritime trade, immigrant communities, and urban development.

Maris was born in the inland town of Alder Springs and grew up in a family with no formal connection to the arts or museums. She first visited a museum during a school trip at the age of ten and developed an early interest in how objects were labeled and arranged. In high school, she volunteered as a helper in the local historical society, where she assisted with simple cataloging tasks such as numbering photographs and filing donor records. These early experiences led her to pursue formal education related to museum work.

Maris earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in History from North Coast College in 2005. During her undergraduate studies, she completed an internship at the campus heritage center, where she helped inventory artifacts from the college’s founding years. She later obtained a Master of Arts in Museum Studies from Lakeshore University in 2008. Her master’s thesis examined low-cost methods for improving collection storage in small museums, with a focus on temperature control, humidity monitoring, and basic pest management.

After completing her graduate degree, Maris accepted a position as an assistant curator at the Riverside Civic Museum, a small institution with limited staff. In this role, she worked directly under the head Museum Curator and gained experience in object handling, database entry, and loan agreements. She was responsible for updating the museum’s object records, photographing items, and creating simple displays about local manufacturing history. Her work at Riverside Civic Museum introduced her to the challenges of balancing public expectations with conservation needs in a small-budget environment.

In 2012, Maris joined the Harborview Museum of Local History as an associate Museum Curator. She was promoted to lead Museum Curator in 2016. As the Museum Curator, she oversees the permanent collection, manages a small curatorial staff, and coordinates with the education and conservation departments. She is responsible for setting collection priorities, approving acquisitions, and ensuring that exhibition content aligns with the museum’s mission. Her curatorial decisions emphasize clear labeling, accessible language, and consistent visual organization.

Maris’s curatorial work at the Harborview Museum includes the redesign of the permanent maritime gallery. She led a multi-year project to reorganize ship models, navigation tools, and trade documents into thematic sections. The new layout groups objects by topic, such as shipbuilding, fishing, and harbor safety, rather than by date alone. She introduced color-coded wall panels to help visitors follow specific themes and added enlarged photographs to connect objects with everyday life in the harbor area. The project also included the installation of upgraded display cases with improved lighting and environmental controls.

As Museum Curator, Maris has developed procedures for evaluating potential donations. She created a checklist that considers an item’s physical condition, connection to local history, and duplication within the existing collection. Under her leadership, the museum has declined large numbers of unrelated objects in order to maintain a clear collecting focus. She has also encouraged the transfer of some items to other institutions better suited to care for them, such as specialized maritime museums or archives.

Maris has played a central role in improving the museum’s collections database. She supervised the migration from an older paper card catalog to a digital system that includes photographs, measurements, and condition notes for each object. She trained staff and volunteers to follow standard naming conventions and to record detailed provenance information when available. This system has allowed the museum to respond more quickly to research requests and to track the movement of objects between storage and exhibition spaces.

In addition to her internal responsibilities, Maris represents the Harborview Museum in professional networks. She attends regional museum association meetings and participates in workshops on topics such as inclusive interpretation, light exposure limits, and emergency planning for collections. She has contributed short articles to newsletters on practical issues faced by small and mid-sized museums, including low-cost mount-making techniques and basic risk assessment for mixed-material displays.

Maris’s work as a Museum Curator extends to community collaboration. She has coordinated temporary exhibitions that draw on objects and stories from neighborhood groups, labor unions, and school projects. For one exhibition on harbor workers, she invited retired dockworkers to help identify tools and equipment in the collection. She also worked with language teachers to translate key labels into multiple languages used in the Harborview area. These projects align with her focus on connecting collection items to the wider community while maintaining curatorial standards for documentation and care.

Within the museum, Maris is known for establishing clear workflows for exhibition planning. She introduced a step-by-step checklist that covers object selection, condition reporting, mount design, label writing, and installation schedules. She requires that each object be examined and documented before it is placed on display and after it is removed, in order to identify any changes in condition. This process supports long-term preservation while allowing frequent updates to gallery content.

Maris continues to serve as the Museum Curator at the Harborview Museum of Local History. Her ongoing projects include reviewing storage areas for overcrowding, planning a small gallery focused on recent immigration to Harborview, and updating emergency response plans for the collection. Her career remains centered on the practical responsibilities of a museum curator: caring for objects, organizing exhibitions, and managing collection information in a way that supports both public access and preservation.
